Rust is everywhere!!

Rust forms when iron is oxidized by oxygen or bacteria

Colourful & magnetic iron minerals

Rust isn't just on old ships, cars or bikes. Rusty iron minerals colour rocks, soils and streams all over the world, including here in Bristol.

Rusty minerals get their colour from the element iron.

They range in colour from red, yellow, green, orange, to black. Some are even magnetic.

Which colour is magnetic?

Slide the magnet along the rail and see which minerals jump onto it!

Meet the tiny rust-makers

Some rust is made by bacteria who breathe iron like we breathe oxygen. Some bacteria make tiny magnetic nanoparticles of the mineral magnetite…

Ancient builders

Bacteria have been doing this for billions of years. Their minerals helped build striped rocks called banded iron formations.

Bacteria with built-in compasses

…but others make magnetic iron minerals inside themselves and swim along the Earth's magnetic field.

Like a compass needle

The chain of magnetic crystals inside each cell lines up with the Earth's magnetic field, just like a compass needle.

Rusty iron is like a sponge

Rusty iron minerals are used for treating water.

They grab hold of pollutants to make it safe to release into the environment.

Try me!

Rusty nails to the rescue

In parts of South East Asia, buckets filled with rusty iron nails are used to remove arsenic from drinking water.

Go magnet fishing!

Tiny magnetic iron minerals stick to pollution like chromium. Move your magnet through the water to fish them out and clean up the pond.
